training set.simple: The part of the data a model learns from. In time series it is the older part.

test set.simple: The part of the data kept hidden to measure how good the model is. In time series it is the newest part.

cutoff.simple: The date that separates training data from test data.
cutoff.example: Cutoff 2024-03-01: all rows before it are training rows.

embargo.simple: A gap of skipped rows between train and test so that overlapping features or labels cannot leak across the cutoff.
embargo.example: A 7-day sum label needs an embargo of 7 days.

backtest.simple: Testing a forecasting method on the past by pretending to forecast from several earlier dates and comparing with what really happened.
backtest.example: Forecast 14 days ahead from 12 different weekly origins.

forecast origin.simple: The last date that is known when a forecast is made. Data after it is hidden from the model.
forecast origin.example: Origin = day 100: you train with days 1 to 100.

horizon.simple: How many steps ahead a forecast looks.
horizon.example: Horizon 7 on daily data means the next 7 days.

mae.simple: Mean absolute error: the average size of the errors, ignoring their sign.

rmse.simple: Root mean squared error: square the errors, average, take the square root. Big errors count more.

quantile.simple: A cut point of a distribution. The 0.9 quantile has 90% of the outcomes below it.
quantile.example: P50 is the median; P90 is the 0.9 quantile.

pinball loss.simple: A score for a quantile forecast. It punishes under- and over-forecasts with different weights, tau and 1 - tau.
pinball loss.example: tau = 0.9, forecast 10 too low: loss 9. Forecast 10 too high: loss 1.

prediction interval.simple: A range that should contain the future value with a stated probability, such as 80%.
prediction interval.example: The 80% interval for tomorrow is 90 to 115.

calibration.simple: How well the stated probabilities match reality. 80% intervals are calibrated if they contain the actual value about 80% of the time.
calibration.example: A 90% interval that covers only 70% of actuals is overconfident.
